title: Christmas Without Ghosts
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 21 of 40
content:
By December, Hogwarts had reopened.

Not completely.

Two corridors remained closed. The Astronomy Tower still had scaffolding. The west greenhouse had been rebuilt but smelled suspiciously of char whenever it rained.

Children returned anyway.

So did noise.

Snape did not return to teaching.

The Board had not decided whether he ever would, and Snape claimed not to care. This was false in at least six observable ways, none of which I was cruel enough to catalogue aloud.

Instead, he occupied the rebuilt research laboratory beside the dungeon classroom and worked on St Mungo's commissions while I finished the last stages of the school audit.

Students knew he was there.

Some were afraid.

Some were curious.

A few Slytherins lingered outside the door as if waiting for a familiar planet to return to orbit.

Snape pretended not to notice.

At Christmas, most students went home.

I stayed because the final contamination report was due in January.

Snape stayed because, according to him, “Travel during holidays is an organized assault on dignity.”

According to McGonagall, he had nowhere he wanted to go.

Christmas morning arrived white and quiet.

I found a box outside my door.

No card.

Inside was a pair of dragon-hide gloves.

Excellent ones.

Black, soft at the fingers, reinforced at the palm. Exactly my size.

I stood in the corridor smiling like an idiot.

Then I looked inside the lid.

A note had been written in small, familiar handwriting.

YOUR CURRENT PAIR IS INFERIOR.

Of course.

I wore them to breakfast.

Snape was already at the end of the staff table with coffee and toast, looking as though Christmas had personally disappointed him.

I sat beside him.

He glanced at the gloves.

“They fit.”

“That sounded dangerously like a question.”

“It was an observation.”

“They're perfect.”

“Good.”

“Thank you.”

His eyes moved toward the ceiling.

“Do not make a spectacle.”

“There are six people in this room.”

“Six too many.”

I smiled.

A small wrapped parcel sat beside my plate.

I slid it toward him.

Snape stared.

“No.”

“Yes.”

“I did not request—”

“Neither did I.”

“That is different.”

“Why?”

He had no answer that did not expose himself.

He took the parcel.

Inside was a fountain pen.

Muggle-made.

Black lacquer, silver nib, weighted for a long hand.

Snape turned it between his fingers.

“What is this?”

“A pen.”

“I can see that.”

“You keep complaining that quills drip on legal forms.”

“They do.”

“This won't.”

He uncapped it.

The expression on his face was almost reverent.

I tried not to look pleased.

“You bought me Muggle stationery.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because it's useful.”

His eyes lifted.

The word held more than it should have.

Useful.

We had talked about that in the pub months before.

What are you when you are not useful?

I added, “And because I thought you'd like it.”

That mattered too.

Snape looked down at the pen.

“I do.”

Two simple words.

They warmed me more than the Great Hall fire.

After breakfast, McGonagall forced everyone remaining in the castle to attend what she called a modest gathering and what Snape called hostage-taking with biscuits.

Flitwick charmed snowflakes to fall indoors without melting. Professor Sprout produced mulled cider. Hagrid brought a pudding large enough to require two people and one levitation charm.

Snape stood near the wall.

I stood beside him.

“You may socialize,” he said.

“So may you.”

“I have chosen not to.”

“Coincidentally, so have I.”

His shoulder brushed mine.

Neither of us moved.

For twenty minutes we watched other people enjoy themselves.

Then Hagrid came over carrying two mugs.

“Happy Christmas, Professor,” he said to Snape.

Snape stiffened.

Hagrid seemed not to notice.

“Not professor at present,” Snape said.

“Still Professor to me.”

The words were gentle and dangerous.

Snape's eyes dropped.

Hagrid handed him a mug.

“Cider. No poison in it.”

Snape looked at me.

I covered my mouth.

Hagrid frowned. “What?”

“Nothing,” I managed.

Snape took the cider.

“Thank you.”

Hagrid smiled and wandered away.

“You have infected him,” Snape murmured.

“With what?”

“Poison jokes.”

“Maybe you're just approachable now.”

His stare suggested I had gone too far.

I laughed.

Later, when the gathering became louder, Snape disappeared.

I found him outside on a covered walkway overlooking the snow.

He did not seem surprised when I joined him.

“Too much Christmas?” I asked.

“Too much humanity.”

“Seasonal condition.”

He leaned against a stone column.

His breath fogged in the cold.

I had brought my coat. He had not.

“You're freezing.”

“I am not.”

“You're in shirtsleeves.”

“I noticed.”

I opened my coat enough to hold one side toward him.

He stared.

“What exactly are you proposing?”

“Shared fabric.”

“This is absurd.”

“Probably.”

He hesitated.

Then stepped closer.

My coat was not large enough to wrap around both of us properly. We ended up shoulder to shoulder beneath one side, ridiculous and warm in patches.

Snape's arm pressed along mine.

I could feel his breathing.

For several minutes, we watched snow settle on the grounds.

“Did you have good Christmases here?” I asked.

His face changed.

“Some.”

“School?”

“Yes.”

“Home?”

“No.”

I nodded.

He looked toward the lake.

“Lily gave me a book once,” he said.

The name no longer shocked the air between us.

“What book?”

“A Muggle book on medicinal plants.”

“That seems perfect.”

“I criticized three inaccuracies.”

“Of course you did.”

“She hit me with it.”

I laughed.

Snape did too, softly.

The memory did not destroy him.

That was new.

“She knew you liked it?”

“Yes.”

His expression softened.

Then sadness passed through it.

I did not try to chase sadness away.

Christmas did not require cheer as proof of healing.

“You can miss her,” I said.

Snape's eyes turned toward me.

“I know.”

The answer surprised me.

Months earlier, I thought he believed grief was a sentence he had to serve.

Maybe he was learning it could simply be grief.

The castle doors opened behind us.

Laughter spilled out.

Snape did not retreat.

His hand moved at his side.

Mine was beside it.

He touched the back of my fingers.

A question.

I turned my hand.

His fingers slid between mine.

We stood like that under the edge of one coat, looking at the snow.

No kiss.

No declaration.

His hand was enough.

After a minute he said, “Your fingers are cold.”

“You're holding them.”

“A tactical error.”

“Release me, then.”

His grip tightened slightly.

“No.”

I smiled toward the grounds.

Inside the castle, someone began singing badly.

Snape closed his eyes in pain.

“Come on,” I said. “We should rescue ourselves.”

“Where?”

“The dungeon. I have contraband biscuits.”

He looked at me.

“Contraband?”

“Stolen from McGonagall.”

His face brightened with wicked approval.

“At last,” he said, “a proper holiday tradition.”

We spent Christmas afternoon in the research lab eating biscuits, testing the fountain pen, and arguing about whether icing sugar constituted contamination.

It was the quietest Christmas I could remember.

Not empty.

Not haunted.

Just quiet.

After dinner, Minerva produced a bottle of whisky old enough to have opinions.

Severus regarded it suspiciously.

“You once drank this willingly,” she said.

“I was younger and surrounded by colleagues.”

“You are currently surrounded by colleagues.”

“That is the problem.”

I accepted a glass. “Coward.”

He looked at me. “You have become reckless with the security of this relationship.”

Minerva's eyebrows rose.

Severus went still.

I bit the inside of my cheek so hard it hurt.

“Relationship?” Minerva repeated mildly.

“Professional,” Severus said.

“Of course.”

“Do not.”

“I said nothing.”

“That has never prevented you from being insufferable.”

Minerva lifted her glass to me. “My sympathies.”

“Thank you.”

“I am sitting here,” Severus said.

“Yes,” we answered together.

For a few seconds the room felt almost ordinary: three adults trading insults after dinner, no armies outside, no school under occupation, no coded allegiance hidden beneath every sentence.

Severus noticed it too. I saw the awareness pass over his face like pain and then become something else.

He raised his glass.

“To uneventful evenings,” he said.

Minerva's expression softened.

I touched my glass to his.

“May we survive the boredom.”

There was a difference.
